source.title: Breaking the Block: Preserving Data Continuity to Train Superior SAEs for Instruct Models
source.authors: Jia-Ming Li; Hao-Ran Ye; Yu-Kun Chen; Xin-Yu Li; Lei Zhang; H. Alinejad-Rokny; Jimmy Chih-Hsien Peng; Min Yang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates whether SAEs yield interpretable features in instruct LLMs, using automated semantic scoring and activation-distribution measures rather than the original toy-model geometry experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses superposition as background and cites Toy Models of Superposition, but does not test toy networks, feature sparsity versus dimensionality, overlap geometry, or capacity allocation. Rows concern the reported SAE feature-interpretability scores for instruct LLMs. Reconstruction, GSNR, and feature-steering results are not rows for these versions: they do not measure superposition or feature recovery directly, and the steering behavior is deliberately induced.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes an SAE training method (FAST) for instruct models. It takes superposition and SAE feature recovery as given: Appendix A frames SAEs as addressing the superposition hypothesis. All reported results compare FAST with block-training baselines on GSNR, MSE, Delta Loss, KL, activation zones and GPT-4o interpretability scores. These measure the paper's own method against others, not whether superposition or recoverable sparse features exist. No toy models, no neuron-level polysemanticity measurement, and no test of feature completeness, stability or dimensionality are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that FAST, which trains SAEs on independent instruction instances rather than concatenated blocks, yields higher GSNR, better reconstruction and behavioral fidelity, and more interpretable features than block training on instruct models. They also conclude that steering special-token features can improve generation quality within a coefficient range. They make no claims testing superposition itself.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains SAEs on instruct-model activations and evaluates feature quality; it does not reproduce the original toy-network setup or its feature-overlap and geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported semantic interpretability differs by SAE training method (FAST, BT(P), BT(F)) and model; the paper also reports different useful coefficient ranges in its deliberately induced steering experiments, which are outside the claim-linked rows.

fits_no_version.finding: Across SAE training methods on instruct LLMs, only a minority of features get high automated monosemanticity scores. Even the best method has 21.1% scored 4–5 on Llama-3.2-3B, and 76.5% score ≤3 on Qwen2.5-3B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The share of SAE features judged interpretable in instruct LLMs depends strongly on the SAE training data pipeline, and remains a minority under the tested setups.

fits_no_version.finding: The distribution of feature maximum activations into weak, effective and unstable zones varies with training method and model. Unstable features fall from about 21% to 1.0% with FAST on Qwen2.5-7B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature activation stability depends on training-data continuity for instruct models.

record.problems: Feature interpretability is assessed by an automated GPT-4o scoring pipeline on top-5 activating contexts; the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for these scores. The highlighted semantic-score comparisons cover limited model/condition examples, and the activation-zone measure is numerical rather than direct evidence of semantic feature recovery.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were created for the extensive reconstruction-MSE, Delta Loss, KL, or GSNR comparisons because these measure SAE reconstruction/training performance rather than any claim version's feature geometry or semantic recovery. No steering rows were included because the paper deliberately induces the outputs and does not report a naturally occurring behavior relevant to these versions.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, or overlap and geometry measurements.
No capacity or importance allocation analysis.
No mechanism for polysemantic neurons is examined.
SAEs are used as a tool. There is no test that features are spread across neurons or that a sparse dictionary is recoverable beyond comparing training methods.
No completeness, cross-seed stability, or canonicality analysis.
No comparison of 1-D directions with multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. The interpretability results are comparisons of the paper's own training method against baselines, with SAEs and superposition assumed as background (Appendix A). All rows are therefore unlinked, and no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-model experiment or measurement of feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry.
No test of capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or sharing of less important features.
No test of non-capacity mechanisms causing polysemantic neurons.

Tests automated semantic interpretability of SAE features in instruct LLMs, but not whether features are distributed across many neurons or whether the reported features are sparse in the underlying model.
Does not establish that SAE features are complete, stable across runs or methods, or canonical units of the model.
No comparison of one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Llama3.2-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Automated semantic scoring of SAE features using top-5 activating contexts; reports share scored 4–5.
rows.note: The semantic scoring rubric rates feature consistency/monosemanticity from 1 to 5.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method (FAST, 21.1% scored 4–5) with baselines. This is method performance, not a test of V4. There is no baseline that could show features are absent.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Automated semantic scoring of SAE features; reports CDF share with scores 1–3.
rows.baseline: BT(P) and BT(F): each reported as over 89%, without separate values
rows.note: The paper reports the baseline comparison only as over 89% for the baselines, without giving separate percentages.
rows.check: Method comparison on Qwen2.5-3B (FAST 76.5% scored ≤3 vs over 89% for baselines). The baseline is the paper's competing methods, so it does not test V4.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The automated semantic evaluation assigns scores 4–5 to 21.1% of FAST features, compared with 7.0% and 10.2% for BT(P) and BT(F), respectively (r1). This is evidence that an SAE can yield some interpretable features in an instruct LLM.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: BT(P) and BT(F) features on Llama3.2-3B-Instruct; FAST features on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
reader_labels.reason: High-quality scores are a minority for the reported Llama model, and the Qwen result reports 76.5% of FAST features at scores ≤3; the paper therefore supports feature recovery only partially and with dependence on training method/model setting (r2–r4).
